transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello there, doc. I, uh... I guess I should just start by saying I wasn't entirely sure about coming in today. You get to be my age, seventy-four years old, and you just sort of figure things are gonna break down or not work the way they used to, you know? But... well, mostly I'm here because I just don't sleep right anymore. It's been driving me absolutely crazy. 

I go to bed, I got my room all set up, nice and quiet, but I just lie there. I lie there for a really long time, tossing and turning, just staring up at the ceiling and watching the shadows from the streetlamp outside. And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it ain't a peaceful rest. I end up waking up from these bad dreams, or sometimes it's just... little noises. Like a floorboard creaking, or the wind hitting the window, or a car driving by a block over. The tiniest little sound and my eyes just pop wide open. 

And the worst part is, once I'm awake like that, I can't seem to settle back down. I try getting up, sitting in my recliner in the living room, maybe having a glass of water, but I just can't get back to sleep no matter what I do. Night after night, it's just... it wears a fella out, not getting any proper rest.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried around bedtime, or does your mind often race with thoughts when you're trying to fall asleep?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I ain't really a worrier, never have been. I mean, I ain't sitting up in bed fretting about the electric bill or if the roof is gonna leak or nothing like that. My mind ain't racing at all. 

Usually, I just watch a little television in the evening—maybe the local news or one of them old Westerns on the classic channel—and I feel right calm, you know? I turn off the set, go in the bathroom to wash my face, brush my teeth... still got most of my own teeth, which ain't too bad for a fella my age... and I get into bed. I get under the covers and my head is just plain quiet. I ain't anxious. I might lay there and think about, oh, I don't know, what I'm gonna make for breakfast the next morning, or if I ought to sweep the front porch, just regular everyday stuff. 

It ain't racing. It's just... wide awake, if you catch my drift. It's like my brain just don't know it's supposed to shut off. So I just lay there, staring at that ceiling, waiting for a sleep that just won't come. And then, like I was saying before, that's when I start hearing every little creak and groan of the house...
Do you usually wake up earlier than you'd like to, and if so, do you find it hard to go back to sleep?

Well, early... see, I don't know about early, exactly. It ain't like I'm waking up at four in the morning when the roosters crow, not that we got roosters around my neighborhood anymore. Old man Miller down the street used to have a few chickens in his backyard, oh, maybe twenty or twenty-five years ago, but the city made him get rid of 'em because of the noise. Caused a whole big fuss, people complaining and all that. 

Anyway, no, I wouldn't say I wake up earlier than I want to in the morning. My regular time to get out of bed has always been about six-thirty, maybe seven. Even back when I was working, doing manual labor, I'd be up by six, so my body is just plain used to that. If I actually make it to the morning, I just get up at my regular time, put my slippers on, and head to the kitchen to get the coffee going. 

The trouble, see, like I was trying to tell you before, is the middle of the night. It ain't the morning that's the problem. It's the two in the morning, three in the morning wake-ups. That's when I pop awake from a bad dream or a floorboard groaning, and then I'm just stuck. I'll go sit in my recliner in the living room, maybe look out the front window at that streetlamp I mentioned, just watching the moths flying around the light. I just sit there for hours, rubbing my knees, wishing I was asleep. But as for the actual morning time? No, I don't wake up too early then. If I'm lucky enough to be asleep when the sun starts coming up, I'll just sleep right till seven like I always have.
Do you find yourself feeling tired or sleepy during the day because of these sleep problems?

Well, you'd think I would be, wouldn't you? What with all that sitting up in the dark and pacing around the living room. But honestly... no, I ain't really sleepy during the daytime. It's the strangest thing. 

I mean, you take my brother-in-law, Frank, for example. He's a year younger than me, seventy-three, and he sleeps like a log all night, but come two in the afternoon, he's dozing off in his armchair. Can't even make it through a whole episode of the game shows without his chin hitting his chest and him snoring away. But me? I've never been much of a napper. Never really had the time for it back when I was working, so I guess I just never got the habit. 

Even with the bad sleep at night now, once the sun is up and I get that first cup of coffee in me, I'm just... I'm awake. I might be a little stiff, you know, my knees and my back ain't exactly what they used to be from all those years hauling things around the work site, but I ain't yawning or feeling like my eyes are heavy. I just go about my day. I'll read the morning paper, maybe go out and tinker a bit in the garage—I got this old push mower I've been meaning to fix up, just needs a little cleaning out, I figure—and I just keep myself moving. So, no, doc, I don't really get tired or sleepy when the sun's out. It's just when the sun goes down that the trouble starts.
When you're lying in bed or sitting quietly at night, do you ever feel an uncomfortable sensation in your legs or a strong urge to move them?

Well, no... no, I can't say that I do. My legs... well, like I said, my knees ache a fair bit, especially when it's damp out or if I've been standing on the concrete floor in the garage too long. That concrete is mighty hard on the joints, you know. I used to wear these thick work boots with the extra padding, but nowadays I just wear my old sneakers, and they don't give much support. 

But as for an uncomfortable feeling... like an urge to move 'em? No, nothing like that. When I'm sitting in my recliner in the middle of the night, my legs are perfectly still. I mean, I might rub my knees, like I told you, just to work the stiffness out, or maybe I'll cross one ankle over the other, but they ain't twitching or restless or nothing. They just sit there like the rest of me, wide awake and waiting for the morning. 

I did know a fella once, guy named Earl I worked with down at the lumber yard... oh, must be thirty years ago now. He used to say his legs felt like they had bugs crawling inside 'em at night. Said he had to get up and walk around the block at two in the morning just to get 'em to settle down. His wife thought he was crazy, going out for a stroll in his pajamas. But me? No, my legs are fine, just a bit stiff from the years. It's just my brain that won't let me sleep, not my legs.
Do you snore loudly or have anyone ever told you that you stop breathing or gasp for air during the night?

Snoring? Well, now... see, since my Mary passed—Lord, it's been six years this November—I've been sleeping alone, mostly. So there ain't nobody right there next to me to complain about it if I do. But even back when she was alive, she never said much about it. Now, my brother-in-law Frank, the one I was telling you about who falls asleep watching the game shows? Oh, he snores like a freight train. You can hear him clear on the other side of the house. His wife, my sister Shirley, she actually makes him sleep in the guest room sometimes when his allergies act up because it gets so loud it rattles the picture frames on the nightstand. 

But me? No, Mary never said I snored loud or nothing. She was a light sleeper, too. If the wind blew too hard against the siding, she'd wake up. But she never poked me in the ribs and told me to roll over or said I was making a racket. And as for stopping breathing or gasping... well, I don't think so. I mean, I'm awake half the night anyway, just sitting there in the dark watching the moths, so I think I'd notice if I suddenly couldn't catch my breath, right? I ain't ever woken up choking or gasping for air. The only thing that wakes me up in a panic is... well, the bad dreams, like I said. But it ain't my breathing that's the problem. It's just my mind running away with me. So, no, doc, I don't think I got any of that going on.
How often do these bad dreams happen—nearly every night, a few times a week, or less often?

Well, doc, that's... that's the whole reason I'm sitting here in this chair today, to be honest with you. Mostly I'm here because I just don't sleep right anymore. It ain't just once in a blue moon, neither. It's... well, it feels like it's all the time. I'll get myself ready for bed, you know, wash my face, brush my teeth, check the locks on the doors—always gotta check the locks, maybe twice, just to be sure—and then I'll get under the covers. And I just lie there. For a long, long time. I'll look at the clock, and it'll be eleven, then twelve, then one. Just staring at the ceiling. 

And then, if I do finally drift off, that's when the dreams come. Or, if it ain't the dreams, it's just... little noises. A branch scraping the window, or a car driving by too fast down on Elm Street. Just the smallest little sound, and my eyes snap open, wide awake, heart beating a little too fast. And once I'm up, whether it's from one of those awful dreams or just a noise in the house... I can't seem to settle back down. I just can't do it. My mind starts racing, and the bed feels too hot, or too cold, or the sheets feel tangled up. So I end up getting out of bed and going out to the living room to sit in my recliner. 

So, how often? It feels like nearly every night, doc. It really does. Some nights are a little better than others, maybe I get a couple hours straight before I wake up, but it's a rare, rare thing for me to just sleep through the night anymore. It's just... I lie there, I wake up, and I can't get back to sleep. That's the long and short of it. I just want to be able to close my eyes and rest like a normal person again, you know?
Can you tell me a little about these bad dreams you mentioned—what they’re about and how they make you feel when you wake up?

Well, doc, the dreams... they're always about the same thing. Always the same awful thing. It’s... well, it’s about the accident. You see, I worked construction most of my life, doing all sorts of jobs, mostly framing and roofing. Hard work, honest work. But this one day, we were working on this big commercial building over on the east side of town—must have been, oh, maybe fifteen years ago now. We were putting up some heavy steel beams, and... well, something gave way. I still don't know exactly what happened, if a cable snapped or what, but the whole thing came down. 

I was underneath, and a piece of the scaffolding collapsed right on top of me. Pinned me down good. I was stuck there for I don't know how long, felt like hours, just smelling the dust and the rust, hearing the metal groaning, wondering if the rest of it was going to come down and finish the job. That’s what the dreams are about. I’m back under there, and it’s dark, and I can’t breathe, and I can’t move my legs. And then I wake up, and my heart is just hammering against my ribs, like a bird trapped in a cage, you know? I’m sweating through my pajamas, and I just feel this... this awful panic, like the ceiling of my own bedroom is about to cave in on me. 

And the thing is, doc, it ain’t just the dreams. It’s not just when I’m sleeping. It happens when I’m wide awake, too. Like, I’ll be walking down the street, maybe going to the hardware store for some nails or something, and I’ll hear a sound. Maybe it’s two pieces of metal scraping together, like a truck hitting a bump, or a gate swinging shut. Or maybe I’ll just see a ladder leaning up against somebody's house, or a pile of pipes sitting in a yard. And just like that, bam. It’s like a switch flips in my brain. Suddenly, I ain't on the sidewalk anymore. The whole thing jumps back in my head, clear as day, like I’m right back under that scaffolding again, waiting for the rescue crew, waiting for help that feels like it’s never going to come. I can almost smell the dust again. It just takes over, you know? And I have to just stand there for a minute and remind myself where I am, that I’m safe, that it’s over. But it doesn't feel over, doc. It really doesn't.
Do you find yourself feeling on edge, easily startled, or having trouble concentrating during the day because of these memories from the accident?

Well, doc, on edge ain't even the half of it. It's like... like my nerves are just sitting right there on the outside of my skin, if you know what I mean. I’m just wound up tight as a cheap watch all day long. And startled? Oh, Lord, yes. It don't take much at all anymore. 

Just the other day, I was down at the grocery store—just that little one down the street, trying to find some of that low-sodium chicken noodle soup because they tell me I gotta watch my salt now at my age—and I was just standing there in the aisle, squinting at the label. And this young fella, I guess he worked there, he just came up behind me to put some boxes on the shelf. He didn't mean no harm, didn't make much noise, but he just stepped up right behind me. 

Well, I tell you, I jumped so hard I nearly dropped the can right there on the linoleum. It's like that with everything now. If a door bangs shut somewhere in the house, or if the wind catches the screen, or if someone just comes up behind me like that grocery boy... I jump hard. I just about jump clear out of my shoes. And the worst part of it is, even after I turn around and see it's just a kid with a box of soup, or just the wind blowing a door, my chest just keeps on thumping. It just thumps and thumps for a good long while. I stand there and tell myself, "You're fine, old man, it's just a noise, it's nothing," but my body just don't listen. It just keeps racing even after I know for a fact it's nothing to worry about. 

Takes me a good ten, fifteen minutes just to get my breath back regular and stop my hands from shaking. So, you can imagine, trying to concentrate on much of anything, whether it's reading the paper or fixing a leaky faucet, when you're jumping at shadows like that... well, it ain't easy. You just sit there waiting for the next thing to bang or crash.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of the accident?

Well, doc, I suppose if I'm being honest with myself, yeah. Yeah, I do. It’s... well, it’s a hard thing to admit, you know, being an old working man and all, but I just keep finding reasons not to do the things I used to do. Take my garage, for instance. I used to spend half my life out there. Built myself a real nice, sturdy workbench out of some scrap oak back in, oh, must've been the late eighties. Had all my tools hung up on one of them pegboards, neat as a pin. I always took pride in keeping my gear in good shape. 

But lately? I just keep finding reasons not to work around the garage. I tell my daughter it's too drafty out there, or my arthritis is acting up in my hands, but the truth of it is... I just don't want to be near it. Especially near the tools. Seeing all that heavy metal, the wrenches and the crowbars... it just doesn't sit right with me anymore. And there's this one spot in the back corner, right next to the side door, where I used to keep that big aluminum extension ladder of mine. I ended up giving the ladder to my son-in-law a while back, but just looking at that empty spot where I used to keep it... I don't know, it just makes my stomach tie up in knots. It reminds me too much of the scaffolding, of the weight of it all. So I just stay inside the house. I figure if something needs fixing, I'll just hire somebody or let it be broken.

And it ain't just the house, neither. I keep finding reasons not to go down to the senior center, too. My buddy Frank, he calls me up almost every Tuesday and Thursday, says they got a pinochle game going, or somebody brought in a box of pastries. And I used to go, I really did. It was good to get out of the house. But... well, a lot of those fellas down there, they're retired tradesmen too, you know? Plumbers, electricians, pipefitters. And they always get to talking about the old days, the jobs they did, the buildings they put up. Or worse, somebody brings up a buddy who got hurt on a site, or a close call they had. And I just... I can't sit there and listen to it. It just brings the whole accident right back up to the front of my mind, plain as day. 

So I make up excuses. I tell Frank I'm expecting a phone call from the insurance company, or I say I got a stomach bug, or I tell him I got chores to do around the house—even though I won't go out to the garage to do 'em. I just stay away. It's just easier, doc, you know? Just staying away from the tools, and the guys who talk about the work, and the places that make me think about it. It just feels safer to stay in my recliner.
Do you find yourself feeling angry, guilty, or fearful about what happened during the accident, or do you blame yourself for it in any way?

Well, doc, as for blaming myself... I don't know if it's blame, exactly. I mean, I was just doing my job that day, same as I always did. I didn't rig up that scaffolding, I was just the guy working underneath it. But fearful? Oh, yeah. Yeah, I got a lot of fear in me now. But the strange thing is, it ain't just fear about the accident itself anymore. It's... well, it's sort of bled into everything else in my life. 

Let me try and explain it to you. You see, when you work with your hands for forty-some years, you learn to trust the things around you. You trust a good piece of oak, you trust the nails you drive, you trust the ground you're standing on. If you build it right, it holds. That's just how the world is supposed to work. But since that day... well, it's like the rules all changed on me. 

I know it may sound foolish, an old man talking like this, but now I keep thinking everyday things aren't safe. I really do. It’s like... if I trust something simple, it'll turn on me. Take the front porch steps at my house, for instance. I poured that concrete myself back in '78. Mixed it right there in the yard, smoothed it out perfect. Solid as a rock. But now, I go to step out in the morning to grab the newspaper, and I look down at that concrete, and my stomach just drops. I start thinking, what if it just crumbles? What if the dirt underneath it washed away in the rain and the whole thing is just waiting to collapse under my boots? 

Or... or the ceiling fan in the living room. My wife bought that at Sears twenty years ago. It's been spinning up there all this time, keeping the room cool, never wobbled once. But I sit in my recliner and look up at it, and my chest gets tight, and I can't help but think those screws are finally gonna snap and the whole heavy mess is gonna come crashing down right on my head. It's exhausting, doc. I can't even trust a regular wooden kitchen chair to hold my weight without wondering if the legs are gonna splinter out from under me. I know a kitchen chair ain't a steel beam, I know my house ain't a construction site, but my brain just won't listen to reason anymore. It just keeps telling me that nothing is safe, nowhere, no how.
Since the accident, do you often feel numb or detached from people, activities, or places that used to matter to you?

Well, doc, "detached" is a mighty good word for it. It’s like... well, let me put it to you this way. My wife, she loves to host a card game. We’ve had this regular group coming over to the house for years now. She sets out the good bowls, puts out some mixed nuts, maybe makes a pot of decaf coffee so we ain't all up all night. And it used to be the highlight of my week, it really did. I'd look forward to it all week long. 

But lately... I don't know. Just this past weekend, they were all over at the house. My wife will be sitting right there, just across the table from me, and the bridge fellows will be joking around, laughing about something in the newspaper or teasing each other about a bad hand they played. And they're loud, too, you know how a bunch of old guys get when they get together and get comfortable. 

But me? I'm sitting right in the middle of it all, and I just feel completely hollowed out. My wife will be sitting right there and the bridge fellows will be joking around, but I feel like I'm behind a window and not really with them. I really do. It's like I'm looking through a thick pane of glass at my own kitchen, just watching them all move their mouths. I can hear the laughing, I can see my wife smiling, but it just doesn't touch me inside. I don't feel the joy of it, I don't feel the fellowship. I just sit there holding my cards, feeling a million miles away. 

I try to nod along, you know, so I don't ruin the evening for everybody else. I don't want my wife worrying over me more than she already does. But the truth of it is, I'm just waiting for them to pack up and go home. It’s a crying shame, doc, because they’re good fellas, salt of the earth types, but I just can't seem to join in no more. I'm just stuck on the other side of that glass.
Since the accident, have you found yourself losing interest in things you used to enjoy, or feeling hopeless about the future?

Well, doc, it ain't exactly that I stopped doing everything. I mean, a man's gotta have something to occupy his time, especially when he's not punching a clock no more and just sitting around the house all day. Take my garden out back, for instance. I got a little patch out there, mostly tomatoes—Beefsteaks and Early Girls, mostly—and some cucumbers and a few bell peppers. I still go out there every morning with the hose. I still water the garden, make sure the soil ain't drying out, pull a weed or two if I see 'em poking up through the mulch. 

But... well, it used to be I'd stand out there in the morning sun, smelling that wet dirt, and I'd just feel... I don't know, peaceful. Content, I guess. I'd get a real good feeling in my chest just watching things grow, knowing I was taking care of 'em. But now? Now I just stand there holding the nozzle, watching the water soak into the dirt, and... nothing. It's just water hitting dirt. The good feeling I used to get from it just doesn't come like it did. It just feels like another chore I gotta get through before I can go back inside and sit down.

And it's the exact same story with my radios. I don't know if I mentioned it before, but I've always liked messing around with electronics. Tinkering with old radios, specifically. The real old ones, you know, the heavy ones with the vacuum tubes and the big wooden cabinets that take up half a table. I got a couple of 'em sitting on the dining room table right now, actually, since I don't go out to the workbench in the garage much anymore. I'll sit there with my soldering iron, replacing a capacitor or trying to get the static to clear up so I can pull a station in from out of state. 

Used to be, when I'd finally hear that music come through the speaker, clear as a bell after hours of messing with the wires, I'd get this rush. A real thrill, like I'd brought something dead back to life. I still tinker with old radios some, I really do... but that thrill is just gone, doc. I fix a connection, the radio plays, the dial lights up, and I just feel flat. It’s like the color’s been washed out of everything. I go through the motions of doing the things I always liked doing, but the joy of it... the joy just packed up and left, I reckon. It makes it mighty hard to look forward to much of anything when even your hobbies feel like just staring at a blank wall.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I'm here because I don't sleep right anymore; I lie there a long time, then wake up from bad dreams or little noises and can't seem to settle back down.

patient.answer:
Well, hello there, doc. I, uh... I guess I should just start by saying I wasn't entirely sure about coming in today. You get to be my age, seventy-four years old, and you just sort of figure things are gonna break down or not work the way they used to, you know? But... well, mostly I'm here because I just don't sleep right anymore. It's been driving me absolutely crazy. 

I go to bed, I got my room all set up, nice and quiet, but I just lie there. I lie there for a really long time, tossing and turning, just staring up at the ceiling and watching the shadows from the streetlamp outside. And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it ain't a peaceful rest. I end up waking up from these bad dreams, or sometimes it's just... little noises. Like a floorboard creaking, or the wind hitting the window, or a car driving by a block over. The tiniest little sound and my eyes just pop wide open. 

And the worst part is, once I'm awake like that, I can't seem to settle back down. I try getting up, sitting in my recliner in the living room, maybe having a glass of water, but I just can't get back to sleep no matter what I do. Night after night, it's just... it wears a fella out, not getting any proper rest.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I ain't really a worrier, never have been. I mean, I ain't sitting up in bed fretting about the electric bill or if the roof is gonna leak or nothing like that. My mind ain't racing at all. 

Usually, I just watch a little television in the evening—maybe the local news or one of them old Westerns on the classic channel—and I feel right calm, you know? I turn off the set, go in the bathroom to wash my face, brush my teeth... still got most of my own teeth, which ain't too bad for a fella my age... and I get into bed. I get under the covers and my head is just plain quiet. I ain't anxious. I might lay there and think about, oh, I don't know, what I'm gonna make for breakfast the next morning, or if I ought to sweep the front porch, just regular everyday stuff. 

It ain't racing. It's just... wide awake, if you catch my drift. It's like my brain just don't know it's supposed to shut off. So I just lay there, staring at that ceiling, waiting for a sleep that just won't come. And then, like I was saying before, that's when I start hearing every little creak and groan of the house...

Therefore, the profile does not cover this specific question.

patient.answer:
Well, early... see, I don't know about early, exactly. It ain't like I'm waking up at four in the morning when the roosters crow, not that we got roosters around my neighborhood anymore. Old man Miller down the street used to have a few chickens in his backyard, oh, maybe twenty or twenty-five years ago, but the city made him get rid of 'em because of the noise. Caused a whole big fuss, people complaining and all that. 

Anyway, no, I wouldn't say I wake up earlier than I want to in the morning. My regular time to get out of bed has always been about six-thirty, maybe seven. Even back when I was working, doing manual labor, I'd be up by six, so my body is just plain used to that. If I actually make it to the morning, I just get up at my regular time, put my slippers on, and head to the kitchen to get the coffee going. 

The trouble, see, like I was trying to tell you before, is the middle of the night. It ain't the morning that's the problem. It's the two in the morning, three in the morning wake-ups. That's when I pop awake from a bad dream or a floorboard groaning, and then I'm just stuck. I'll go sit in my recliner in the living room, maybe look out the front window at that streetlamp I mentioned, just watching the moths flying around the light. I just sit there for hours, rubbing my knees, wishing I was asleep. But as for the actual morning time? No, I don't wake up too early then. If I'm lucky enough to be asleep when the sun starts coming up, I'll just sleep right till seven like I always have.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive daytime sleepiness or fatigue due to poor sleep, which would help distinguish between insomnia disorder and another sleep-wake disorder.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling tired or sleepy during the day because of these sleep problems?

target_item.reason: The symptom profile does not contain information about whether the patient experiences daytime sleepiness or fatigue as a result of their sleep problems.

patient.answer:
Well, you'd think I would be, wouldn't you? What with all that sitting up in the dark and pacing around the living room. But honestly... no, I ain't really sleepy during the daytime. It's the strangest thing. 

I mean, you take my brother-in-law, Frank, for example. He's a year younger than me, seventy-three, and he sleeps like a log all night, but come two in the afternoon, he's dozing off in his armchair. Can't even make it through a whole episode of the game shows without his chin hitting his chest and him snoring away. But me? I've never been much of a napper. Never really had the time for it back when I was working, so I guess I just never got the habit. 

Even with the bad sleep at night now, once the sun is up and I get that first cup of coffee in me, I'm just... I'm awake. I might be a little stiff, you know, my knees and my back ain't exactly what they used to be from all those years hauling things around the work site, but I ain't yawning or feeling like my eyes are heavy. I just go about my day. I'll read the morning paper, maybe go out and tinker a bit in the garage—I got this old push mower I've been meaning to fix up, just needs a little cleaning out, I figure—and I just keep myself moving. So, no, doc, I don't really get tired or sleepy when the sun's out. It's just when the sun goes down that the trouble starts.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any physical discomfort or urge to move during rest periods, which may indicate restless legs syndrome or another condition contributing to nighttime wakefulness.
doctor.question: When you're lying in bed or sitting quietly at night, do you ever feel an uncomfortable sensation in your legs or a strong urge to move them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of Restless Legs Syndrome (uncomfortable sensations in the legs and an urge to move them), which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Well, no... no, I can't say that I do. My legs... well, like I said, my knees ache a fair bit, especially when it's damp out or if I've been standing on the concrete floor in the garage too long. That concrete is mighty hard on the joints, you know. I used to wear these thick work boots with the extra padding, but nowadays I just wear my old sneakers, and they don't give much support. 

But as for an uncomfortable feeling... like an urge to move 'em? No, nothing like that. When I'm sitting in my recliner in the middle of the night, my legs are perfectly still. I mean, I might rub my knees, like I told you, just to work the stiffness out, or maybe I'll cross one ankle over the other, but they ain't twitching or restless or nothing. They just sit there like the rest of me, wide awake and waiting for the morning. 

I did know a fella once, guy named Earl I worked with down at the lumber yard... oh, must be thirty years ago now. He used to say his legs felt like they had bugs crawling inside 'em at night. Said he had to get up and walk around the block at two in the morning just to get 'em to settle down. His wife thought he was crazy, going out for a stroll in his pajamas. But me? No, my legs are fine, just a bit stiff from the years. It's just my brain that won't let me sleep, not my legs.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of sleep apnea, such as snoring or breathing interruptions during sleep, which could explain nighttime awakenings and lack of restful sleep.
doctor.question: Do you snore loudly or have anyone ever told you that you stop breathing or gasp for air during the night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of sleep apnea, such as snoring loudly or gasping for air during sleep, which are not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Snoring? Well, now... see, since my Mary passed—Lord, it's been six years this November—I've been sleeping alone, mostly. So there ain't nobody right there next to me to complain about it if I do. But even back when she was alive, she never said much about it. Now, my brother-in-law Frank, the one I was telling you about who falls asleep watching the game shows? Oh, he snores like a freight train. You can hear him clear on the other side of the house. His wife, my sister Shirley, she actually makes him sleep in the guest room sometimes when his allergies act up because it gets so loud it rattles the picture frames on the nightstand. 

But me? No, Mary never said I snored loud or nothing. She was a light sleeper, too. If the wind blew too hard against the siding, she'd wake up. But she never poked me in the ribs and told me to roll over or said I was making a racket. And as for stopping breathing or gasping... well, I don't think so. I mean, I'm awake half the night anyway, just sitting there in the dark watching the moths, so I think I'd notice if I suddenly couldn't catch my breath, right? I ain't ever woken up choking or gasping for air. The only thing that wakes me up in a panic is... well, the bad dreams, like I said. But it ain't my breathing that's the problem. It's just my mind running away with me. So, no, doc, I don't think I got any of that going on.

doctor.intent: Assess the presence and frequency of bad dreams to determine if they are a significant contributor to the patient's sleep disturbance.
doctor.question: How often do these bad dreams happen—nearly every night, a few times a week, or less often?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Mostly I'm here because I don't sleep right anymore; I lie there a long time, then wake up from bad dreams or little noises and can't seem to settle back down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of the bad dreams, which are explicitly mentioned in the manifestation of the patient's sleep disturbance.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, that's... that's the whole reason I'm sitting here in this chair today, to be honest with you. Mostly I'm here because I just don't sleep right anymore. It ain't just once in a blue moon, neither. It's... well, it feels like it's all the time. I'll get myself ready for bed, you know, wash my face, brush my teeth, check the locks on the doors—always gotta check the locks, maybe twice, just to be sure—and then I'll get under the covers. And I just lie there. For a long, long time. I'll look at the clock, and it'll be eleven, then twelve, then one. Just staring at the ceiling. 

And then, if I do finally drift off, that's when the dreams come. Or, if it ain't the dreams, it's just... little noises. A branch scraping the window, or a car driving by too fast down on Elm Street. Just the smallest little sound, and my eyes snap open, wide awake, heart beating a little too fast. And once I'm up, whether it's from one of those awful dreams or just a noise in the house... I can't seem to settle back down. I just can't do it. My mind starts racing, and the bed feels too hot, or too cold, or the sheets feel tangled up. So I end up getting out of bed and going out to the living room to sit in my recliner. 

So, how often? It feels like nearly every night, doc. It really does. Some nights are a little better than others, maybe I get a couple hours straight before I wake up, but it's a rare, rare thing for me to just sleep through the night anymore. It's just... I lie there, I wake up, and I can't get back to sleep. That's the long and short of it. I just want to be able to close my eyes and rest like a normal person again, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine the content and emotional tone of the bad dreams to assess for possible PTSD or other anxiety-related disorders contributing to sleep disturbance.
doctor.question: Can you tell me a little about these bad dreams you mentioned—what they’re about and how they make you feel when you wake up?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I hear metal scrape or see a ladder leaning in somebody's yard, the whole thing jumps back in my head like I'm under there again waiting for help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the content of the bad dreams, which are a form of re-experiencing the trauma. This falls under intrusive symptoms, where the patient recalls the traumatic event.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, the dreams... they're always about the same thing. Always the same awful thing. It’s... well, it’s about the accident. You see, I worked construction most of my life, doing all sorts of jobs, mostly framing and roofing. Hard work, honest work. But this one day, we were working on this big commercial building over on the east side of town—must have been, oh, maybe fifteen years ago now. We were putting up some heavy steel beams, and... well, something gave way. I still don't know exactly what happened, if a cable snapped or what, but the whole thing came down. 

I was underneath, and a piece of the scaffolding collapsed right on top of me. Pinned me down good. I was stuck there for I don't know how long, felt like hours, just smelling the dust and the rust, hearing the metal groaning, wondering if the rest of it was going to come down and finish the job. That’s what the dreams are about. I’m back under there, and it’s dark, and I can’t breathe, and I can’t move my legs. And then I wake up, and my heart is just hammering against my ribs, like a bird trapped in a cage, you know? I’m sweating through my pajamas, and I just feel this... this awful panic, like the ceiling of my own bedroom is about to cave in on me. 

And the thing is, doc, it ain’t just the dreams. It’s not just when I’m sleeping. It happens when I’m wide awake, too. Like, I’ll be walking down the street, maybe going to the hardware store for some nails or something, and I’ll hear a sound. Maybe it’s two pieces of metal scraping together, like a truck hitting a bump, or a gate swinging shut. Or maybe I’ll just see a ladder leaning up against somebody's house, or a pile of pipes sitting in a yard. And just like that, bam. It’s like a switch flips in my brain. Suddenly, I ain't on the sidewalk anymore. The whole thing jumps back in my head, clear as day, like I’m right back under that scaffolding again, waiting for the rescue crew, waiting for help that feels like it’s never going to come. I can almost smell the dust again. It just takes over, you know? And I have to just stand there for a minute and remind myself where I am, that I’m safe, that it’s over. But it doesn't feel over, doc. It really doesn't.

inference.note: The patient provided detailed descriptions of recurrent nightmares related to a past traumatic event (construction accident), as well as intrusive thoughts and flashbacks triggered by external stimuli. These symptoms strongly suggest Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), which is now added as a candidate (F43.10). Insomnia disorder (G47.00) remains a candidate due to the persistent difficulty falling and staying asleep. The patient does not endorse symptoms of anxiety at bedtime, ruling out anxiety-related sleep disturbance as a primary cause. No evidence of substance use, mood episodes, or other primary sleep disorders such as sleep apnea or restless legs syndrome were endorsed.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of post-traumatic stress related to the accident during the day, such as persistent negative emotional state, irritability, or difficulty concentrating.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling on edge, easily startled, or having trouble concentrating during the day because of these memories from the accident?

target_item.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
target_item.manifestation: If a door bangs or someone comes up behind me, I jump hard and my chest keeps thumping for a while even after I know it's nothing.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient is 'easily startled', which corresponds to the exaggerated startle response symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, on edge ain't even the half of it. It's like... like my nerves are just sitting right there on the outside of my skin, if you know what I mean. I’m just wound up tight as a cheap watch all day long. And startled? Oh, Lord, yes. It don't take much at all anymore. 

Just the other day, I was down at the grocery store—just that little one down the street, trying to find some of that low-sodium chicken noodle soup because they tell me I gotta watch my salt now at my age—and I was just standing there in the aisle, squinting at the label. And this young fella, I guess he worked there, he just came up behind me to put some boxes on the shelf. He didn't mean no harm, didn't make much noise, but he just stepped up right behind me. 

Well, I tell you, I jumped so hard I nearly dropped the can right there on the linoleum. It's like that with everything now. If a door bangs shut somewhere in the house, or if the wind catches the screen, or if someone just comes up behind me like that grocery boy... I jump hard. I just about jump clear out of my shoes. And the worst part of it is, even after I turn around and see it's just a kid with a box of soup, or just the wind blowing a door, my chest just keeps on thumping. It just thumps and thumps for a good long while. I stand there and tell myself, "You're fine, old man, it's just a noise, it's nothing," but my body just don't listen. It just keeps racing even after I know for a fact it's nothing to worry about. 

Takes me a good ten, fifteen minutes just to get my breath back regular and stop my hands from shaking. So, you can imagine, trying to concentrate on much of anything, whether it's reading the paper or fixing a leaky faucet, when you're jumping at shadows like that... well, it ain't easy. You just sit there waiting for the next thing to bang or crash.

inference.note: The patient described symptoms consistent with PTSD (F43.11), including recurrent nightmares related to a traumatic event (the construction accident), intrusive memories, hypervigilance, being easily startled, and significant distress. These symptoms were not fully explored in prior turns and now meet diagnostic criteria. Insomnia disorder (G47.00) remains a candidate given the persistent difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient avoids situations that remind him of the accident, which would support a diagnosis of PTSD.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of the accident?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I keep finding reasons not to go to the senior center or work around the garage, especially near the tools and the spot where I used to keep that ladder.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about avoiding places, people, or activities that remind me of the accident, which matches the Trauma Avoidance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, I suppose if I'm being honest with myself, yeah. Yeah, I do. It’s... well, it’s a hard thing to admit, you know, being an old working man and all, but I just keep finding reasons not to do the things I used to do. Take my garage, for instance. I used to spend half my life out there. Built myself a real nice, sturdy workbench out of some scrap oak back in, oh, must've been the late eighties. Had all my tools hung up on one of them pegboards, neat as a pin. I always took pride in keeping my gear in good shape. 

But lately? I just keep finding reasons not to work around the garage. I tell my daughter it's too drafty out there, or my arthritis is acting up in my hands, but the truth of it is... I just don't want to be near it. Especially near the tools. Seeing all that heavy metal, the wrenches and the crowbars... it just doesn't sit right with me anymore. And there's this one spot in the back corner, right next to the side door, where I used to keep that big aluminum extension ladder of mine. I ended up giving the ladder to my son-in-law a while back, but just looking at that empty spot where I used to keep it... I don't know, it just makes my stomach tie up in knots. It reminds me too much of the scaffolding, of the weight of it all. So I just stay inside the house. I figure if something needs fixing, I'll just hire somebody or let it be broken.

And it ain't just the house, neither. I keep finding reasons not to go down to the senior center, too. My buddy Frank, he calls me up almost every Tuesday and Thursday, says they got a pinochle game going, or somebody brought in a box of pastries. And I used to go, I really did. It was good to get out of the house. But... well, a lot of those fellas down there, they're retired tradesmen too, you know? Plumbers, electricians, pipefitters. And they always get to talking about the old days, the jobs they did, the buildings they put up. Or worse, somebody brings up a buddy who got hurt on a site, or a close call they had. And I just... I can't sit there and listen to it. It just brings the whole accident right back up to the front of my mind, plain as day. 

So I make up excuses. I tell Frank I'm expecting a phone call from the insurance company, or I say I got a stomach bug, or I tell him I got chores to do around the house—even though I won't go out to the garage to do 'em. I just stay away. It's just easier, doc, you know? Just staying away from the tools, and the guys who talk about the work, and the places that make me think about it. It just feels safer to stay in my recliner.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms include chronic sleep disturbance and nightmares related to a traumatic event (construction accident), as well as hypervigilance, avoidance behaviors, and intrusive memories. These findings support a diagnosis of PTSD (F43.11). No new candidates were added, and insomnia disorder (G47.00) remains a possible contributing factor to sleep difficulties, though the trauma-related nature of the nightmares and awakenings makes PTSD the more prominent diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has persistent negative emotional state (e.g., fear, anger, guilt) related to the trauma, which would support PTSD diagnosis.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself feeling angry, guilty, or fearful about what happened during the accident, or do you blame yourself for it in any way?

target_item.name: Negative_Beliefs
target_item.manifestation: I know it may sound foolish, but now I keep thinking everyday things aren't safe and that if I trust something simple, it'll turn on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative emotions such as anger, guilt, or fear, and whether the patient blames himself for the accident, which corresponds to the negative beliefs and distorted cognitions about the trauma.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, as for blaming myself... I don't know if it's blame, exactly. I mean, I was just doing my job that day, same as I always did. I didn't rig up that scaffolding, I was just the guy working underneath it. But fearful? Oh, yeah. Yeah, I got a lot of fear in me now. But the strange thing is, it ain't just fear about the accident itself anymore. It's... well, it's sort of bled into everything else in my life. 

Let me try and explain it to you. You see, when you work with your hands for forty-some years, you learn to trust the things around you. You trust a good piece of oak, you trust the nails you drive, you trust the ground you're standing on. If you build it right, it holds. That's just how the world is supposed to work. But since that day... well, it's like the rules all changed on me. 

I know it may sound foolish, an old man talking like this, but now I keep thinking everyday things aren't safe. I really do. It’s like... if I trust something simple, it'll turn on me. Take the front porch steps at my house, for instance. I poured that concrete myself back in '78. Mixed it right there in the yard, smoothed it out perfect. Solid as a rock. But now, I go to step out in the morning to grab the newspaper, and I look down at that concrete, and my stomach just drops. I start thinking, what if it just crumbles? What if the dirt underneath it washed away in the rain and the whole thing is just waiting to collapse under my boots? 

Or... or the ceiling fan in the living room. My wife bought that at Sears twenty years ago. It's been spinning up there all this time, keeping the room cool, never wobbled once. But I sit in my recliner and look up at it, and my chest gets tight, and I can't help but think those screws are finally gonna snap and the whole heavy mess is gonna come crashing down right on my head. It's exhausting, doc. I can't even trust a regular wooden kitchen chair to hold my weight without wondering if the legs are gonna splinter out from under me. I know a kitchen chair ain't a steel beam, I know my house ain't a construction site, but my brain just won't listen to reason anymore. It just keeps telling me that nothing is safe, nowhere, no how.

inference.note: The patient described symptoms consistent with PTSD (F43.11) due to the traumatic construction accident and subsequent re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal symptoms. The insomnia and sleep disruption initially pointed toward Nonorganic Insomnia (G47.00). This turn added F43.12 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic) as the patient's symptoms have persisted for many years and are consistently tied to the traumatic event, with no indication of resolution or recent onset.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent negative emotional state related to the accident, which would help distinguish between adjustment disorder (F43.2) and PTSD (F43.1).
doctor.question: Since the accident, do you often feel numb or detached from people, activities, or places that used to matter to you?

target_item.name: Social_Detachment
target_item.manifestation: My wife will be sitting right there and the bridge fellows will be joking around, but I feel like I'm behind a window and not really with them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling numb or detached from people, which directly corresponds to the symptom of social detachment.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, "detached" is a mighty good word for it. It’s like... well, let me put it to you this way. My wife, she loves to host a card game. We’ve had this regular group coming over to the house for years now. She sets out the good bowls, puts out some mixed nuts, maybe makes a pot of decaf coffee so we ain't all up all night. And it used to be the highlight of my week, it really did. I'd look forward to it all week long. 

But lately... I don't know. Just this past weekend, they were all over at the house. My wife will be sitting right there, just across the table from me, and the bridge fellows will be joking around, laughing about something in the newspaper or teasing each other about a bad hand they played. And they're loud, too, you know how a bunch of old guys get when they get together and get comfortable. 

But me? I'm sitting right in the middle of it all, and I just feel completely hollowed out. My wife will be sitting right there and the bridge fellows will be joking around, but I feel like I'm behind a window and not really with them. I really do. It's like I'm looking through a thick pane of glass at my own kitchen, just watching them all move their mouths. I can hear the laughing, I can see my wife smiling, but it just doesn't touch me inside. I don't feel the joy of it, I don't feel the fellowship. I just sit there holding my cards, feeling a million miles away. 

I try to nod along, you know, so I don't ruin the evening for everybody else. I don't want my wife worrying over me more than she already does. But the truth of it is, I'm just waiting for them to pack up and go home. It’s a crying shame, doc, because they’re good fellas, salt of the earth types, but I just can't seem to join in no more. I'm just stuck on the other side of that glass.

inference.note: This turn added F43.10 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, unspecified) due to the patient's persistent avoidance behavior, intrusive memories, hypervigilance, and emotional detachment following a traumatic construction accident. These symptoms align with PTSD criteria and were not fully captured in previous candidates which focused on adjustment and insomnia disorders.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent negative emotional state (e.g., depression) related to the accident, which would help differentiate between PTSD and adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Since the accident, have you found yourself losing interest in things you used to enjoy, or feeling hopeless about the future?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I still water the garden and tinker with old radios some, but the good feeling I used to get from it just doesn't come like it did.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities and an inability to feel positive emotions or hope, which aligns with the symptom of persistent inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, it ain't exactly that I stopped doing everything. I mean, a man's gotta have something to occupy his time, especially when he's not punching a clock no more and just sitting around the house all day. Take my garden out back, for instance. I got a little patch out there, mostly tomatoes—Beefsteaks and Early Girls, mostly—and some cucumbers and a few bell peppers. I still go out there every morning with the hose. I still water the garden, make sure the soil ain't drying out, pull a weed or two if I see 'em poking up through the mulch. 

But... well, it used to be I'd stand out there in the morning sun, smelling that wet dirt, and I'd just feel... I don't know, peaceful. Content, I guess. I'd get a real good feeling in my chest just watching things grow, knowing I was taking care of 'em. But now? Now I just stand there holding the nozzle, watching the water soak into the dirt, and... nothing. It's just water hitting dirt. The good feeling I used to get from it just doesn't come like it did. It just feels like another chore I gotta get through before I can go back inside and sit down.

And it's the exact same story with my radios. I don't know if I mentioned it before, but I've always liked messing around with electronics. Tinkering with old radios, specifically. The real old ones, you know, the heavy ones with the vacuum tubes and the big wooden cabinets that take up half a table. I got a couple of 'em sitting on the dining room table right now, actually, since I don't go out to the workbench in the garage much anymore. I'll sit there with my soldering iron, replacing a capacitor or trying to get the static to clear up so I can pull a station in from out of state. 

Used to be, when I'd finally hear that music come through the speaker, clear as a bell after hours of messing with the wires, I'd get this rush. A real thrill, like I'd brought something dead back to life. I still tinker with old radios some, I really do... but that thrill is just gone, doc. I fix a connection, the radio plays, the dial lights up, and I just feel flat. It’s like the color’s been washed out of everything. I go through the motions of doing the things I always liked doing, but the joy of it... the joy just packed up and left, I reckon. It makes it mighty hard to look forward to much of anything when even your hobbies feel like just staring at a blank wall.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms, including recurrent nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance behaviors, hypervigilance, and emotional numbing following a traumatic event (construction accident), strongly point to PTSD (F43.11). Other candidates (e.g., insomnia disorder, adjustment disorder, or another anxiety disorder) are less likely given the specificity and duration of trauma-related symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a clear history of trauma (construction accident involving collapse of scaffolding and life-threatening entrapment) followed by persistent re-experiencing symptoms (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance of trauma-related stimuli (garage, construction tools, social events with fellow tradesmen), negative alterations in cognition and mood (detachment, anhedonia, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, pervasive sense of unsafety), and marked hyperarousal (elevated startle response, hypervigilance, difficulty falling and staying asleep). These symptoms have persisted for more than 15 years and result in clinically significant distress and functional impairment across multiple domains.
